section_summary: This section comprises diplomatic despatches, military intelligence reports, telegrams, and memoranda from January to June 1941 concerning Japanese internal politics and foreign relations. Key topics include evaluations of Prince Konoye's administration and the reorganization of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association into a non-political spiritual mobilization group, alongside the secret peace initiative submitted to President Roosevelt by Bishop James E. Walsh and Father Drought. The documents also trace Japanese diplomatic maneuvers surrounding the Soviet-Japanese Neutrality Pact, the mediated settlement of the Indochina-Thailand border dispute, military operations in south and central China, and internal tensions arising from anti-foreign agitation and the outbreak of the Russo-German war.

subfiles.about: Conclusion of a military intelligence report on the career, character, and British connections of Lieutenant General Masaharu Homma.
subfiles.summary: This page concludes a biographical military report on Lieutenant General Masaharu Homma, noting his appointments as Commander of the Japanese Defense Forces in Tientsin in 1939 and Commander of the Taiwan Army in 1940. It highlights his extensive service in England with the British Army, his English fluency, and his sociable demeanor with foreigners. The report observes that despite Homma's distaste for international complications, he was placed in command during the tense Japanese blockade of the foreign concessions at Tientsin.
subfiles.title: Military Attaché Report No. 10,305: Lieutenant General Masaharu Homma

subfiles.about: Biographical outline of the military background and career of General Shigeru Hasunuma upon his appointment as Chief Aide-de-Camp to the Emperor.
subfiles.summary: This military report outlines the career of General Shigeru Hasunuma from his graduation from the Military Academy in 1904 through his service in the Russo-Japanese War, World War I observer missions in Europe, and staff roles in Siberia. It traces his advancement through senior cavalry and division commands in Manchuria and North China to his 1939 appointment as Chief Aide-de-Camp to the Emperor and promotion to full general in 1940. Lieutenant Colonel Creswell notes that although Hasunuma has stayed out of the public eye, he is highly regarded within the army and his imperial appointment received general press approval.
subfiles.title: Military Attaché Report No. 10,306: General Shigeru Hasunuma

subfiles.about: Internal Department of State routing note concerning the revision of the Diffendorfer memorandum and inquiries regarding Father Bitter.
subfiles.summary: This brief handwritten Division of Far Eastern Affairs routing slip notes that the memorandum of conversation with Dr. Diffendorfer was revised in accordance with Dr. Hornbeck's suggestions. It also states that inquiries were initiated to determine whether the Department had any existing reports concerning Father Bitter, a German Jesuit active in Japan.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Note on Father Bitter and Memorandum Revision

subfiles.about: Account by Dr. Ralph E. Diffendorfer of his impressions during a visit to Japan and Korea, focusing on totalitarian trends and the withdrawal of American personnel.
subfiles.summary: Dr. Ralph E. Diffendorfer of the Methodist Board of Foreign Missions recounts his recent survey of conditions in Japan and Korea, reporting that extreme nationalist factions and German-inspired youth groups were aggressively driving Japan toward totalitarianism. He describes interviews with Ambassador Grew, Korean leaders, and Foreign Minister Matsuoka, who insisted that Japan would not leave China and warned the United States to stay on its own side of the Pacific. Convinced of imminent peril, Diffendorfer planned to urge his mission board and the International Missionary Council to withdraw all American missionaries, an action supported by Japanese Christian leaders like Bishop Abe. He also discusses Father Bitter, a German Jesuit who frequently visited the United States to solicit funds for Catholic work in Japan.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation: Dr. Diffendorfer's Account of His Recent Impressions

subfiles.about: Instruction transmitting to the American Embassy in Tokyo a copy of the memorandum of conversation with Dr. Ralph E. Diffendorfer.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary of State transmits to Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo, for confidential staff information, the February 17, 1941 memorandum of conversation with Dr. Ralph E. Diffendorfer. The enclosure records Dr. Diffendorfer's observations on the Japanese internal situation and his recommendations regarding the evacuation of American citizens from Japan.
subfiles.title: Instruction to the American Ambassador at Tokyo Transmitting Memorandum of Conversation with Dr. Diffendorfer

subfiles.about: Fortnightly summary of Far Eastern political, diplomatic, and military affairs prepared for the Secretary of State.
subfiles.summary: This comprehensive Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum reviews major Far Eastern developments for Secretary Hull, noting mounting Japanese domestic dissatisfaction with Prince Konoye's government and the Imperial Rule Assistance Association. It analyzes the Japanese-dictated mediation settlement of the Indochina-Thailand border conflict and the departure of Foreign Minister Matsuoka for Moscow, Berlin, and Rome to seek a political accord with the Soviet Union. It also examines Soviet-Japanese commercial deadlocks, Japan's cautious attitude toward southward expansion, rubber export quotas, Japanese bombing of American missionary property in Honan, troop withdrawals in Kwangtung, traffic on the Burma Road, and friction between Chiang Kai-shek and the Chinese Communists.
subfiles.title: The Situation in the Far East (Division of Far Eastern Affairs Summary)

subfiles.about: Fragmented telegraphic report on instructions issued to Japanese Consul General Hayashi in Hanoi concerning evacuation in view of tense peace talks.
subfiles.summary: This fragmentary telegram transmits Japanese news dispatches and Domei reports indicating that Consul General Baron Yasukichi Hayashi in Hanoi was instructed regarding the Indochina-Thailand peace negotiations. Citing a threatened breakdown in the Tokyo mediation talks, Hayashi was reportedly directed to order the immediate evacuation of Japanese residents from Indochina.
subfiles.title: Telegram on Japanese Evacuation Orders in French Indochina

subfiles.about: President Roosevelt's memorandum asking Secretary Hull for his opinion on Bishop Walsh's peace proposal.
subfiles.summary: President Franklin D. Roosevelt forwards to Secretary of State Cordell Hull a confidential memorandum recently presented to him by Bishop James E. Walsh. The President requests Hull's advice on what action the United States government should take regarding the proposals.
subfiles.title: Memorandum for the Secretary of State from President Roosevelt on Bishop Walsh's Proposal

subfiles.about: Strictly confidential proposal submitted by Bishop Walsh outlining terms for a comprehensive settlement between Japan and the United States.
subfiles.summary: This confidential memorandum, drafted by Bishop Walsh and Father Drought following discussions with Japanese leaders, argues that moderate Japanese leaders, including Prince Konoye and the Emperor, wish to extricate Japan from the China War and modify their international alignments if supported by the United States. It outlines a proposed agreement under which Japan would reinterpret its Axis commitments to avoid war with America, settle the China conflict based on terms previously offered by Chiang Kai-shek, and agree to a Far Eastern Monroe Doctrine guaranteeing the status of the Philippines, Singapore, Malaya, and the Dutch East Indies. In exchange, the United States would provide economic cooperation, including a large gold credit, reciprocal trade, and Open Door guarantees. The memorandum urges President Roosevelt to secretly dispatch a trusted personal representative to Tokyo to negotiate a final pact directly with Japanese leaders.
subfiles.title: Strictly Confidential Memorandum for President Roosevelt: Proposal for Japanese-American Settlement

subfiles.about: Secretary Hull's memorandum to President Roosevelt advising against pursuing Bishop Walsh's peace initiative and recommending standard diplomatic channels.
subfiles.summary: Secretary of State Cordell Hull advises President Roosevelt that Bishop Walsh's proposed plan is impracticable and unlikely to be accepted in good faith by the Japanese government. Hull warns that assisting Japan to extricate itself from China would likely encourage Japanese military aggression southward rather than redirect it toward peaceful processes. He recommends awaiting the imminent arrival of Japanese Ambassador-designate Nomura and working through established diplomatic channels and Ambassador Grew in Tokyo rather than utilizing informal intermediaries.
subfiles.title: Memorandum for the President from Secretary Hull Regarding Bishop Walsh's Proposals

subfiles.about: Detailed State Department analysis examining the fundamental fallacies and hazards of Bishop Walsh's proposed Japanese-American agreement.
subfiles.summary: This detailed memorandum, prepared under the supervision of Stanley K. Hornbeck, evaluates Bishop Walsh's peace proposals against the realities of Japanese military dominance since 1931. It argues that Japanese military leaders are committed to conquest and that relieving Japanese forces in China would merely facilitate a rapid military drive toward the richer resources of Southeast Asia. The memorandum systematically critiques the legal, political, and economic provisions of the plan, pointing out that Japan is unlikely to make meaningful unilateral commitments, that a Far Eastern Monroe Doctrine is legally and geographically untenable, and that peace is impossible without genuine Japanese cessation of aggression and respect for Chinese sovereignty.
subfiles.title: Detailed Memorandum for the President on Bishop Walsh's Proposals Regarding Japan

subfiles.about: Technical annex analyzing subordinate aspects of Bishop Walsh's peace proposal, including territorial guarantees and Chinese prerequisites.
subfiles.summary: This annex provides specific commentary on secondary provisions of Bishop Walsh's plan, pointing out that extending a Japanese-American guarantee over Southeast Asian territories contradicts long-standing United States foreign policy. It examines the difficulties of establishing autonomous regimes in Indochina and the Netherlands East Indies under international sanction while noting their current semi-autonomous operations. Finally, it stresses that the Chinese government will not enter negotiations without concrete indications of Japanese good faith, specifically a withdrawal of Japanese expeditionary troops from China.
subfiles.title: Comments on Subordinate Aspects of the Proposed Plan (Annex)

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing Ambassador Grew's monthly report on Japanese internal political affairs for February 1941.
subfiles.summary: This State Department cross-reference file note indexes Despatch No. 5461, dated March 24, 1941, from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo. The original document, filed under 894.00 P.R./158, provides a monthly report on Japanese internal political affairs for February 1941.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet: Despatch No. 5461 on Japanese Internal Political Affairs

subfiles.about: Department of State file charge-out sheet recording that decimal file paper 894.00/1035 was returned to the Adviser on Political Relations.
subfiles.summary: This file sheet indicates that the document catalogued under decimal file number 894.00/1035 was returned to the office of the Adviser on Political Relations (PA/H, Stanley K. Hornbeck). No underlying correspondence or memorandum text is included in the file.
subfiles.title: File Sheet for 894.00/1035: Returned to PA/H

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting on a mass rally in Tokyo held by the newly established Tohokai political party led by Seigo Nakano.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports on an inaugural mass meeting of ten thousand people held by the Tohokai, the first political party established since the dissolution of parties in 1940. Led by Seigo Nakano, the party issued a declaration urging the Japanese government to take decisive foreign policy action based on its diplomatic advantages under the Tripartite Pact and the Soviet-Japanese neutrality treaty. It strongly advocated stabilizing the southern regions as an absolute prerequisite for constructing Greater East Asia.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 630 from Tokyo on the Organization of the Tohokai Party

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting on a prominent editorial in the Kokumin newspaper warning Japan against the insidious dangers of National Socialism.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew summarizes an editorial in the Tokyo vernacular paper Kokumin that cautioned the Japanese nation against the menace of National Socialism. The article argued that while communism was recognized as dangerous and democracy maintained balance through competing parties, National Socialism was insidiously overlooked despite its fifth-column methods that paralyzed European nations. It concluded that Japan must seriously reflect on the danger and avoid attempting to imitate an organization and power structure that it cannot replicate.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 644 from Tokyo Reporting Kokumin Editorial on National Socialism

subfiles.about: Summary memorandum by the Division of Far Eastern Affairs on Despatch No. 5528 regarding official efforts to curb anti-foreign agitation in Japan.
subfiles.summary: This Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum summarizes Tokyo Despatch No. 5528, reporting that Vice Minister for Foreign Affairs Chuichi Ohashi admonished the Japanese public against hostility toward foreigners and instructed police officers to be courteous. It notes editorial support in vernacular newspapers and highlights Ambassador Grew's hope that these official efforts will help curtail the xenophobic tendencies previously encouraged by the press and government.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Summary of Despatch No. 5528 on Anti-Foreign Agitation

subfiles.about: Despatch reporting Vice Foreign Minister Chuichi Ohashi's address to prefectural governors urging courtesy toward foreigners and curbing xenophobia.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports on a speech delivered on April 10, 1941, by Vice Minister for Foreign Affairs Chuichi Ohashi before a conference of prefectural governors, in which Ohashi condemned anti-foreign hatred as unworthy of a great nation and contrary to Bushido. Ohashi specifically admonished police officers to treat law-abiding foreign residents with courtesy rather than unnecessary harassment. Grew observes that the statement implicitly rebuked Japanese police behavior and notes supportive editorial commentary in major vernacular newspapers, enclosing an editorial translation from the Japan Times and Advertiser.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 5528: Anti-Foreign Agitation in Japan - Foreign Vice-Minister Chuichi Ohashi's Remarks

subfiles.about: Summary memorandum by the Division of Far Eastern Affairs on Despatch No. 5551 analyzing the reorganization of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association.
subfiles.summary: This Division of Far Eastern Affairs summary analyzes Tokyo Despatch No. 5551 concerning the reorganization of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association announced on April 12. It points out that the abolition of the Diet, Planning, and Policy Bureaux removed potential conflicts with the Diet and reduced the association to a spiritual mobilization organ. The memorandum notes that this shift reflects resistance to totalitarian restructuring while cautioning that it does not signify a revival of liberalism or a change in Japan's foreign policy.
subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs Summary of Despatch No. 5551 on Reorganization of the IRAA

subfiles.about: Despatch analyzing the structural reorganization and political decline of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew provides a detailed assessment of the drastic reorganization of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association announced on April 12, 1941, following severe criticism from the Diet over its constitutional ambiguities and political ambitions. The reform involved the mass resignation of staff, Count Arima's replacement by Heisuke Yanagawa and Sotaro Ishiwata, and the abolition of the Diet, Planning, and Policy Bureaux, effectively reducing the IRAA to an administrative and spiritual mobilization body. Grew emphasizes that this outcome symbolizes Prince Konoye's failure to establish a totalitarian internal structure and highlights the resurgence of political party impulses, including Seigo Nakano's Tohokai and the Diet Members Club, though he cautions that foreign policy objectives remain unchanged.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 5551: The Reorganization of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing a telegram regarding a confidential message sent to Baron Hiranuma concerning a potential Cabinet crisis.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference file note indexes Telegram No. 718 sent from Tokyo on May 21, 1941, by Ambassador Joseph C. Grew. The original document, filed under 711.94/2118, reports on a confidential message conveyed to Baron Kiichiro Hiranuma requesting that the fall of the Konoye Cabinet be arranged should a crisis occur in United States-Japanese relations.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet: Telegram No. 718 on Message to Baron Hiranuma

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting the resignation of Tadaatsu Ishiguro as Minister of Agriculture and Forestry and the appointment of Hiroyasu Ino.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that Tokyo newspaper extras announced the resignation of Tadaatsu Ishiguro as Minister of Agriculture and Forestry due to poor health. Vice Minister Hiroyasu Ino was designated as his successor. The Embassy indicates that no broader political significance is attached to this ministerial replacement.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 806 from Tokyo on Resignation of Agriculture Minister Ishiguro

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting proceedings of the Cooperative Council of the IRAA, including criticism of government policy in Southeast Asia and press commentary.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports on the opening session of the Cooperative Council of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association, where Chairman Admiral Nobumasa Suetsugu urged delegates to speak critically and openly. Member of Parliament Shinzo Imai attacked the government's indecisive stance in economic negotiations with the Netherlands East Indies and called for a forceful southward advance while condemning pro-Anglo-American elements. The telegram also surveys editorial reactions in Tokyo newspapers regarding national spirit, council debates, and government-public harmony.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 833 from Tokyo on Cooperative Council of the Imperial Rule Assistance Association

subfiles.about: British Embassy memorandum reporting Japanese trade protests in Hong Kong and Soviet Foreign Commissar Molotov's reassurances to China.
subfiles.summary: This memorandum from the British Embassy in Washington transmits intelligence from an April 24 London telegram. It reports renewed Japanese representations against British export restrictions on scrap iron and gall nuts from Hong Kong. It also reveals that Soviet Foreign Commissar Molotov assured the Chinese Ambassador that the Russo-Japanese Neutrality Pact had no bearing on China, that recognition of Manchukuo and Outer Mongolia merely acknowledged existing facts, and that Soviet transport of war supplies to China would continue unimpeded.
subfiles.title: British Embassy Memorandum on Hong Kong Trade Restrictions and Soviet Assurances to China

subfiles.about: Fortnightly summary of Far Eastern affairs reviewing the diplomatic and military consequences of the Russo-Japanese Neutrality Pact.
subfiles.summary: This Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum examines the international situation following Foreign Minister Matsuoka's return to Tokyo after signing the neutrality pact in Moscow. It reports Japanese coastal offensives in Chekiang and Fukien resulting in the capture of Ningpo and Foochow to tighten the blockade of China, while noting Baron Hiranuma's confidential assurance that Japan intended to pursue only peaceful southward expansion unless subjected to foreign blockade or economic pressure. The review also discusses ongoing Soviet-Japanese commercial negotiations, heavy German shipments of locomotives, submarines, and aircraft machinery to Manchuria, growing Gestapo activity in Japan, and the arrival of 2,000 U.S. Army reinforcements in Manila.
subfiles.title: The Situation in the Far East (Division of Far Eastern Affairs Summary)

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting a press interview in Tokyo given by Wang Ching-wei proposing an East Asiatic Axis and collaboration with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew summarizes a press interview given in Tokyo by Wang Ching-wei, head of the Nanking collaborationist regime. Wang advocated the formation of an immutable East Asiatic Axis and an East Asia League for Racial, Military, and Political Cooperation, asserting that Nanking would establish a model peace zone with Japanese assistance. He claimed that Chungking and the Chinese Communists were not genuinely cooperating and predicted the eventual downfall of communism, while indicating that measures to strengthen the Nanking government were being prepared.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 860 from Tokyo on Wang Ching-wei's Press Interview

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing a telegram regarding the current status of political affairs in Japan.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference file note indexes Telegram No. 852 sent on June 19, 1941, by Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo. The original document, filed under 762.9411/270, contains information concerning the present status of various political affairs in Japan.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet: Telegram No. 852 on Political Affairs of Japan

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing a telegram reporting on British diplomatic assessments of Foreign Minister Matsuoka's political influence.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference note indexes Telegram No. 808, dated June 11, 1941, from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew. The original telegram, filed under 762.9411/267, quotes a paraphrase of a June 8 message sent to London by British Ambassador Craigie regarding a rally to support Foreign Minister Matsuoka and analyzes Matsuoka's political power to carry the Cabinet with him during an international crisis.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet: Telegram No. 808 on Foreign Minister Matsuoka's Political Strength

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting recommendations submitted to Prime Minister Konoye by Kenzo Adachi representing Admiral Suetsugu's political faction.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports that Cabinet Councilor Kenzo Adachi, representing Admiral Suetsugu's newly named Council for Launching National Policies, called upon Prime Minister Konoye to deliver recommendations regarding national policy. The telegram notes that Cabinet councilors were scheduled to confer collectively with Konoye on July 1 and underscores the importance of individual councilors pressing foreign policy advice during the international crisis.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 898 from Tokyo on Cabinet Councilors' Recommendations to Prime Minister Konoye

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing a telegram reporting Japanese Cabinet difficulties resulting from the outbreak of the Russo-German war.
subfiles.summary: This cross-reference note indexes Telegram No. 879 sent by Ambassador Joseph C. Grew on June 25, 1941. The original paper, filed under 740.0011 European War, 1939/12479, reports intelligence indicating that the Konoye Cabinet was encountering acute political and strategic difficulties following the German invasion of the Soviet Union.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet: Telegram No. 879 on Cabinet Difficulties over the Russo-German War

subfiles.about: Cover letter from FBI Director J. Edgar Hoover transmitting an intelligence memorandum on Japanese activities to Assistant Secretary Berle.
subfiles.summary: Federal Bureau of Investigation Director J. Edgar Hoover transmits a confidential memorandum concerning Japanese activities to Assistant Secretary of State Adolf A. Berle, Jr. The communication was delivered by special messenger for the Department's information.
subfiles.title: Letter from J. Edgar Hoover to Adolf A. Berle, Jr. Transmitting Memorandum on Japanese Activities
